1. What's actually required to get a Steam Web API key today — process, whether it's instant/free, any approval gate. Fetch https://steamcommunity.com/dev/apiterms and report the actual current terms text, including the 100,000 calls/day limit and any "personal, non-commercial use" language. Also check https://steamcommunity.com/dev to see the actual key-request form/process.
2. For these ~10 games — ARK: Survival Evolved, Garry's Mod, Project Zomboid, CS2, Killing Floor 2, Unturned, Don't Starve Together, Conan Exiles, Space Engineers, Barotrauma — research whether there's ANY Steam Web API endpoint or documented method to determine programmatically whether a given Steam appid has anonymous/dedicated-server Workshop downloads enabled (i.e. can a dedicated server pull workshop content without a logged-in Steam user). Search Steamworks documentation (partner.steamgames.com), SteamCMD docs, and community sources (e.g. developer.valvesoftware.com wiki). Confirm or refute: does this require empirical per-app testing because no such API/flag exists?
3. Research `IPublishedFileService/QueryFiles/v1` (part of Steam Web API) — fetch https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/webapi/IPublishedFileService or search for its documentation. Confirm: does this endpoint work with just a Steam Web API key for searching/browsing Workshop items? Contrast with `ISteamRemoteStorage/GetPublishedFileDetails` which reportedly doesn't need a key — confirm that distinction with real docs.

## Part B: mod.io deep dive
1. What games does mod.io actually support today? Fetch https://mod.io/games or their public games list page, and report real games listed, noting any overlap with these Nxeon-hosted games: Minecraft, Valheim, Rust, Palworld, CS2, Terraria, ARK: Survival Evolved/Ascended, Satisfactory, Project Zomboid, 7 Days to Die, V Rising, Enshrouded, Factorio, Garry's Mod, Conan Exiles, Unturned, The Forest, Sons of the Forest, Dragonwilds, Sunkenland, Abiotic Factor, Core Keeper, Icarus, Soulmask, Don't Starve Together, Vintage Story, Necesse, TF2, Left 4 Dead 2, Nightingale, Squad, Space Engineers, Killing Floor 2, Barotrauma, Insurgency Sandstorm, Mordhau, The Isle, Stationeers, Eco, Empyrion.
2. Fetch https://docs.mod.io (their API docs landing / getting started page) — report real auth requirements (API key vs OAuth), real rate limits if documented, and what fields a mod record contains (does it include a license field, images/gallery, download URLs, file metadata)?
3. Fetch https://mod.io/legal/aup (Acceptable Use Policy) and any page about commercial use / reseller terms (search "mod.io reseller license", "mod.io enhanced license", "mod.io commercial terms"). Quote the actual relevant text about commercial/reseller use.
4. Is there a real, current contact path for API access — a specific email, developer signup form, or partner contact page? Check https://mod.io/business or similar and report what you actually find (don't guess an email).

Organize your response as Part A (Steam) and Part B (mod.io), citing real URLs throughout. Flag uncertainty explicitly rather than guessing. Be information-dense, this feeds a larger report.

API keys linked to a game have unlimited requests. API keys linked to a user have 60 requests per minute. User tokens are limited to 120 requests per minute.

Exceeding the rate limit will result in requests receiving a 429 Too Many Requests response until the reset time is reached.

mod.io implements rate limiting to stop users abusing the service. They enforce global rate limits which will result in all requests being blocked (error ref 11008). They also enforce per-endpoint rate limits which will only result in requests to that endpoint being blocked (error ref 11009) until the duration specified in the retry-after header (in seconds) passes, allowing you to continue to call other endpoints.

## Handling Rate Limits

It is highly recommended you architect your app to check for the 429 Too Many Requests HTTP response code, and ensure you do not continue to make requests until the duration specified in the retry-after header (in seconds) passes.

The retry-after header specifies the number of seconds before you can attempt to make another request to API.

Users who continue to send requests despite a 429 Too Many Requests response could potentially have their credentials revoked.

# Part A: Steam Workshop — Practical Verification

## A1. Getting a Steam Web API key

- **Process**: The key-request form is at `https://steamcommunity.com/dev/apikey` (linked from the docs landing page `https://steamcommunity.com/dev`). Note: this URL required an authenticated Steam login when fetched anonymously (it resolved to a Steam login/account-verification interstitial), confirming the key request is tied to a logged-in Steam account, not an open public form. I could not independently verify from that page whether a "domain name" field is mandatory or whether the key issues instantly — this is a known behavior from general Steam documentation/community knowledge, but I was not able to confirm the domain-field requirement with a fetched primary source, so treat that specific detail as **unconfirmed** by this research pass.
- `https://steamcommunity.com/dev` documentation states: "All use of the Steam Web API requires the use of an API Key" and "Use of the APIs also requires that you agree to the Steam API Terms of Use," directing users to the apikey form. (https://steamcommunity.com/dev)
- **Terms of Use** (`https://steamcommunity.com/dev/apiterms`), key provisions actually found on the page:
  - Call limit: **"You are limited to one hundred thousand (100,000) calls to the Steam Web API per day."**
  - The terms do **not** contain explicit "personal, non-commercial use only" language as a blanket restriction — instead they grant a license to "access the Steam Web API, implement the Steam Web API in your Application, and distribute Steam Data to end users," subject to a list of prohibited uses (no implying Valve endorsement/affiliation, no violating the Steam Subscriber Agreement, no degrading Steam's operation, no unfair multiplayer advantage tech, no unsolicited marketing use of the data, no storing user passwords/intercepting Steam auth, no sharing API keys with third parties).
  - Valve retains broad, unilateral termination rights: "Valve may change, suspend or discontinue the Steam Web API and suspend or terminate your use of the Steam Web API, Steam Data, and/or Valve Brand & Links at any time for any reason, without notice."
  - Material breaches must be reported to `webapi@valvesoftware.com`.
  - (https://steamcommunity.com/dev/apiterms)
- **Conclusion**: getting a key itself appears free and self-service (no visible manual approval gate in the docs), but it requires a logged-in Steam account, and Valve's terms leave wide latitude to revoke access at will — there's no guaranteed "commercial license" status, just a permissive-but-revocable grant.

## A2. Does a public API/flag exist to tell if an appid supports anonymous dedicated-server Workshop downloads?

**No such API/flag was found. This has to be verified empirically per game**, and here's the evidence:

- The actual mechanism is a **developer-side, per-app Steamworks setting**, not something queryable by a third party. Per Steamworks partner documentation workflow (confirmed via search of partner.steamgames.com content and community sources): a game's publisher must log into Steamworks at `https://partner.steamgames.com/apps/workshop/[appid]`, go to "Technical tools" → "Edit Steamworks settings" → "Workshop" tab, and check **"Enable anonymous game servers to download workshop items."** This is a private, publisher-only toggle — there is no public Web API method or SteamCMD command to query its current state for a given appid.
- Practically, hosts/admins determine this by trial: attempting `steamcmd +login anonymous +app_update <serverid> +workshop_download_item <appid> <workshopid> +quit` and seeing whether the download succeeds or is empty/fails. Multiple sources confirm this by-experiment approach:
  - Barotrauma has an open GitHub issue about `workshop_download_item` failing with anonymous login (https://github.com/FakeFishGames/Barotrauma/issues/7707) — i.e., Barotrauma is a case where anonymous Workshop download does **not** work (mods must be pre-packaged/subscribed via an authenticated account or bundled by the server operator), matching community reports.
  - Community/hosting-provider docs for ARK: Survival Evolved, Project Zomboid, and Conan Exiles each independently confirm anonymous SteamCMD login does work for pulling Workshop content on those specific titles (e.g., Project Zomboid's dedicated server app, appid 380870, installs and downloads workshop content anonymously; Conan Exiles servers commonly use `login anonymous` for workshop mod downloads).
  - General guidance from AlliedModders and other server-admin communities: "SteamCMD lets you download Workshop content anonymously for most free-to-play games, though paid [non-F2P] games may require login" — i.e., behavior is inconsistent and title-specific, reinforcing that there's no documented universal rule or API flag.
- I did not find any Valve developer-wiki (developer.valvesoftware.com) page that exposes this as a documented, queryable flag; the SteamCMD wiki page (https://developer.valvesoftware.com/wiki/SteamCMD) documents the anonymous-login mechanism generically but not a per-app capability lookup.

**Confirmed conclusion for the report**: there is no Steam Web API, SteamCMD command, or public Steamworks endpoint to programmatically determine whether a given appid has anonymous-server Workshop downloads enabled. It is a private per-title Steamworks checkbox set by the developer, and the only reliable way to know is to actually attempt an anonymous `workshop_download_item` call against a real, subscribed-and-public workshop item for that appid and observe success/failure. Budget for manual, empirical per-game verification of all ~10 target titles (ARK: Survival Evolved, Garry's Mod, Project Zomboid, CS2, Killing Floor 2, Unturned, Don't Starve Together, Conan Exiles, Space Engineers, Barotrauma) rather than assuming API-based detection is possible.

## A3. `IPublishedFileService/QueryFiles/v1` vs `ISteamRemoteStorage/GetPublishedFileDetails`

- **`IPublishedFileService/QueryFiles/v1`** (https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/webapi/IPublishedFileService): documented as performing "a search query for published files," taking `query_type`, `page`/`cursor`, `creator_appid`/`appid`, `requiredtags`/`excludedtags`/`search_text`, `filetype`, and response-shaping flags (`return_vote_data`, `return_tags`, `return_previews`, etc.). Its `key` parameter is listed as a **required** "Steamworks Web API user authentication key" — so yes, it works with a standard Steam Web API key (the documentation does not flag it as publisher-only, unlike sibling methods in the interface such as `Delete`, `SetDeveloperMetadata`, and `UpdateBanStatus`, which explicitly require a publisher key). This makes it usable for searching/browsing Workshop items for a given appid with just a normal key — useful for building a mod catalog browser.
- **Contrast: `ISteamRemoteStorage/GetPublishedFileDetails`** (https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/webapi/ISteamRemoteStorage): its parameter table does **not** list a `key` parameter at all, meaning it is callable without authentication (publicly/anonymously). This confirms the commonly cited distinction: `GetPublishedFileDetails` (and `GetCollectionDetails`) are public, keyless lookups for details of a *specific known* published-file ID, while `IPublishedFileService/QueryFiles` is the actual search/browse mechanism and does require a Web API key. Note: some third-party/community sources (e.g., search snippets referencing "publisher API key" for `GetPublishedFileDetails`) conflict with the official doc's parameter table — I'm flagging this as a minor discrepancy worth a final manual confirmation against a live call, since one general web search result asserted the opposite (that it requires a publisher key and must be server-side).
